section_title: Understanding the heat loss of your property
label: Sections and elevations show your ceiling heights and window sizes. If you don't have them, tell us room by room below.
step_intro: To size the heating for each room we need to know how much heat your home loses. If you're not sure of something, choose the closest option; your Project Engineer checks every answer.

section_title: Understanding the heat loss of your property
label: Do you have up-to-date section and elevation drawings?
options: yes=Yes|no=No, I'll give the heights room by room|standard=No, please use standard heights
why: Elevations show what the outside walls look like, to scale. Windows and doors lose heat faster than walls, so we use their sizes to make sure the system suits the space. Sections are a slice through the building: they show ceiling heights, split levels and vaulted areas. Rooms with high ceilings hold more air to heat. The standard ceiling height is 2.4 m.

section_title: Understanding the heat loss of your property
label: Ceiling heights, room by room
why: A good set of plans includes sections showing ceiling heights. Without them we need the height of every room and any vaulted areas, because the room volume sets its heat requirement.
placeholder: e.g. 2.4 m everywhere except the kitchen-diner, vaulted to 4.2 m

section_title: Understanding the heat loss of your property
label: Window and external door sizes, room by room
why: Elevations show windows and doors to scale. With only floor plans we have the widths but not the heights, and glazing is where most heat is lost.
placeholder: e.g. living room: 4 m bifold doors, 2.1 m high; bedrooms: 1.2 m × 1.2 m

section_title: Understanding the heat loss of your property
label: How well your walls, windows, roof and floor hold heat sets how much heat each room needs. Choose the easiest way to tell us: a SAP calculation, your EPC, typical values for the age of your home, or describe each part yourself. You can change any card.

section_title: Understanding the heat loss of your property
label: How would you like to tell us about the insulation?
options: sap=Upload my SAP calculation|epc=Find my EPC|typical=Typical for the age of my property|describe=I'll describe it

section_title: Heating and controls
label: Where would you like the manifold(s)?
why: Each manifold feeds the pipe loops around it, so its position sets how the loops are laid out and how far the pipe runs. A cupboard near the middle of the floor it serves is ideal. Mark them on the plans if it's easier to show than to say.
step_intro: Where the manifolds go, where we shouldn't heat, and a few details about your floors.
placeholder: e.g. utility room cupboard, and the airing cupboard upstairs. Or: marked on the plans

section_title: Heating and controls
label: Anywhere we shouldn't heat?
why: We keep pipe out from under fitted units, islands, baths, showers and staircases. A kitchen or bathroom drawing, even a sketch, stops us heating under your island.
placeholder: e.g. under the kitchen island and the bath. Garage and plant room unheated. Open staircase.

section_title: Heating and controls
label: Screed: liquid or hand-mixed, and the depth
why: Liquid screed flows round the pipe and can be thinner; hand-mixed needs more depth over the pipe. The depth sets how quickly the floor warms up.
placeholder: e.g. liquid screed, 50 mm over the pipe

section_title: Heating and controls
label: Are there steels, notches or unusual joists we should know about?

section_title: Heating and controls
label: Joisted floors: joist type, direction and spacing, and any steels
hint: Joist type: Posi, TJI/I-joist, Eco or traditional timber. If the joist layout is on your plans, just say so. Steels: where they are and whether there's a 25 mm gap above or below them.
why: We draw the pipe between the joists, so we need their direction and spacing in each room. Engineered joists (Eco, TJI, Posi) let the pipe cross anywhere. Traditional timber joists have to be notched or battened, which limits where it can cross. Steels need a 25 mm gap for the pipe to pass, or they must be drilled, which your structural engineer has to agree.
placeholder: e.g. I-joists front to back at 400 mm centres; one steel over the kitchen with a gap above

section_title: Heat pump information required for MCS
label: What type of heat pump are you installing?
options: ashp=Air source heat pump|loop=Ground source heat pump with ground loop array|bore=Ground source heat pump with borehole
step_intro: Where your heat pump and its equipment will go, and how it sits in relation to your neighbours. We use this for the MCS noise check, which is part of signing your installation off.

section_title: Heat pump information required for MCS
label: Have you got a plan which shows the location of the heat pump?
options: plans=Already provided on floor plans|yes=Yes, I'll upload it|no=I'll describe its location
why: Air source heat pumps (ASHPs) require a certain amount of free space around them in order to operate efficiently. As well as providing space for airflow, this space is also used as access for commissioning and servicing. You can find the make and model of your heat pump on your quote. An air source heat pump must be more than 1 m from the boundary to count as permitted development (3 m in Wales). Closer than that needs a planning application.
